issues.legal_issue: Agricultural income arising under a settlement is attributable to the settlor when the settlement reserves a power to cancel or alter it and thereby reassume control over the assets or income.
material_facts: The settlor executed a deed giving the beneficiary a life interest in agricultural lands and providing for the lands to pass to the settlor’s children after her death, or to revert to the settlor or his heirs if there were no such children.
The deed reserved the settlor’s right to cancel, revoke, or alter the settlement in specified circumstances, including circumstances requiring cancellation or alteration.
The agricultural income from the lands was included in the settlor’s assessable income, and the administrative and High Court reviews upheld that inclusion.
issues.conclusion: The settlement was a revocable transfer, so the income from the lands was properly included in the settlor’s agricultural income; the later interests in the children did not alter that result.
issues.legal_principle: Section 9(1), including its first proviso, treats income from a revocable transfer as the transferor’s income and treats a settlement as revocable when it gives the settlor a right to reassume power over the assets or income. The third proviso’s exclusion is for qualifying settlements that are not revocable for the specified period or lifetime and from which the settlor derives no direct or indirect benefit. The court held the reserved power fell within the first proviso. It assumed the gift was valid and did not rely on section 126 of the Transfer of Property Act to determine its validity. No earlier case was relied on for this issue.

predicates.income_arose_under_settlement: The income arose from assets placed under a settlement.
predicates.settlor_reserved_power_to_cancel_or_alte: The settlement reserved to the settlor a power to cancel or alter it, allowing the settlor to reassume control over the assets or income.

issues.definition: When agricultural income arises under a settlement in an assessment proceeding and the settlor reserved a power to cancel or alter the settlement, the income is attributed to the settlor.

issues.legal_issue: A challenge to the validity of a taxing provision cannot be determined in a revision or reference arising from a decision of taxing authorities that lack jurisdiction to consider that validity.
material_facts: The assessee sought to raise a constitutional challenge to the provision in an appeal following a revision from the taxing authorities’ decision.
The taxing authorities were not empowered to consider whether the taxing provision was ultra vires.
The assessee also relied on the Supreme Court’s constitutional powers, but the court found no basis to decide the challenge in this appeal.
issues.conclusion: The court declined to entertain the constitutional challenge in this proceeding, leaving it open to be raised in an appropriate proceeding.
issues.legal_principle: Under K.S. Venkataraman & Co. v. State of Madras, taxing authorities are not concerned with the validity of taxing provisions, and a validity challenge is outside their jurisdiction; the High Court or Supreme Court cannot determine that challenge in a revision or reference from those authorities. The court followed Commissioner of Income-tax v. Straw Products Ltd. It noted that Sardar Baldev Singh v. Commissioner of Income-tax and Balaji v. Income-tax Officer had left a similar validity question open. Article 142 did not enable the court to decide the issue in this appeal.

issues.definition: When a validity challenge arises in review of a taxing authority’s decision and that authority could not decide validity, the reviewing court does not entertain the challenge in that proceeding.

issues.legal_issue: Reliance on a rule governing revocation of gifts does not defeat attribution of income under a tax rule when the settlement itself reserves a power to cancel or alter it.
material_facts: The settlor relied on section 126 of the Transfer of Property Act in relation to the settlement.
The deed expressly reserved the settlor’s power to cancel, revoke, or alter the settlement.
The court assumed the gift was valid and decided the income-attribution issue on the basis of the reserved power.
issues.conclusion: Section 126 did not assist the assessee because, even assuming the gift was valid, the settlor had specifically retained the power to cancel, revoke, or alter the settlement.
issues.legal_principle: The court did not decide whether section 126 applied or whether the gift was valid; it assumed validity and held that the expressly reserved power remained relevant to the tax treatment of the income under section 9(1). No earlier case was relied on for this point.
